extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of moral philosophy, intellectual history, and the history of European morals
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of ancient views on death
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the distinct ethical doctrines, social tactics, and moral standards concerning death, suicide, and virtue as presented in a historical survey of Stoicism, Epicureanism, and patristic Christianity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation for death as a chief philosophical end
rubrics_metrics.description: The preparation for death was deemed one of the chief ends of philosophy; constant meditation on death was used to detach the mind from fortune and to extinguish superstitious terrors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: assists detachment from life's gifts, produces placid courage and self-reliant majesty (Stoic ideal). Anti-patterns / cautions: excessive preoccupation forces death into unhealthy prominence, forms an unnaturally tense and tragical character, annihilates ambition and enthusiasm, and may cast a chill over the affections. (Bacon and Spinoza cited as critics.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of living over dying (Spinoza's corrective)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper study of a wise man is not how to die, but how to live; the sage will think less about death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: active duty and engagement in life are the best preparation for death; excessive contemplation of death tends to defeat its object by increasing fear and diminishing life's active virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death as natural rest / indifference (Stoic/Epicurean view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient philosophers commonly regarded death as a natural rest or as indifferent — either extinguishing sensation (so no evil) or emancipating the soul — and attributed terrors of death to diseased imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and authorities: Epicurus ('death is indifferent'), Cicero, Seneca. Use in consolatory literature: arguments that death either secures happiness or ends suffering; metaphors like extinguished candle. Purpose: to remove superstitious terror and free the individual from fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolation literature and appeals to immortality
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical 'Consolations' deployed arguments about death and sometimes, especially in Cicero and Plutarch, appealed to the immortality of the soul as an additional motive for comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction: Cicero and Plutarch incorporate immortality more prominently than Stoics; Plutarch sometimes bases consolation on oracles and Bacchic mysteries rather than pure philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular superstition vs philosophical rationalism about death
rubrics_metrics.description: Where philosophers sought to dispel fears, the popular mind retained vivid notions of infernal torments, auguries, visions, and other fables that made death a subject of dread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Greek vases and poems depict infernal tortures; Lucretius and Plutarch 'On Superstition' trace these terrors. Implication: philosophical teaching aimed at destroying these popular terrors as a chief function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian/patristic doctrine: death as penal consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Patristic and medieval Catholic teaching represented death as a penal infliction introduced by Adam's sin, often accompanied by doctrines of punishment (hell, purgatory) and a fundamentally fallen human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: this view is radically different from pagan thought; it fostered an attitude that death itself is revolting and appalling and thus became a tool for ecclesiastical moral government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priestly strategy: magnify terrors of death to secure submission
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church used legends, ceremonies, art, dogma, and ritual (e.g., inhumation rather than cremation, depictions of decay, visions of purgatory) to emphasize the loathsomeness and punitive aspects of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: by concentrating imagination on ghastliness and eternal torment, ecclesiastical culture converted fear of death into an instrument of governance and prepared people to accept church consolations and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical permissiveness toward suicide in antiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ancient philosophers (notably Stoics and some Epicureans) recognized a general right to dispose of one's own life, especially as a rational response to intolerable suffering, old age, or dishonor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Seneca and other Stoics advocate suicide as refuge from oppression or hopeless disease; Lucretius and others practiced or praised suicide; arguments framed suicide as euthanasia or escape from tyranny. Legal practice: generally tolerated in Rome with limited later restrictions (Domitian, Hadrian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic and moral objections to suicide (counterarguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authorities (Pythagoras, Plato in some contexts, Aristotle) condemned suicide on religious or civic grounds—as disobedience to divine command, abandonment of duty, or injury to the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual limits: Plato permitted suicide in some cases (e.g., when law required it); Aristotle's condemnation is grounded in harm to the polity. Later Roman law imposed specific restrictions (suicide of an accused person could equate to condemnation; soldiers' suicides treated as desertion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic ethical system: reason and will as sole principle of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoicism taught that reason reveals a law of nature and that the will, controlled by reason, is the sole principle of virtue; emotions are treated as diseases and virtue is pursued irrespective of reward or punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications for conduct: dignity comes from conforming to nature and regarding death without dismay; suppression of desires and strengthening of will are central. Effect: produces an austere, self-reliant moral ideal consonant with certain social types (e.g., Roman military).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social formation of moral types: military influence on Roman ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Roman civic and military institutions shaped a distinct moral excellence—frugal, honourable, laborious, courageous—favoring heroism, self-restraint, and contempt for suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relation to Stoicism: Stoic ethics fit and reinforce these pre-existing Roman virtues; the social context both produced and sustained the Stoical ideal of independent morals and readiness to accept or choose death.
